newsitem.title: ISRAEL: US mounts Mideast peace rescue, Arab leaders wary.
newsitem.headline: US mounts Mideast peace rescue, Arab leaders wary.

text.p: Arab leaders were wary on Thursday over prospects of reviving the stalled Middle East peace process soon, although the U.S. unveiled plans to try rescue it.
The State Department said U.S. special Middle East envoy Dennis Ross will return to the region next week in an effort to get the peace process back on track.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat's spokesman, Marwan Kanafani, said the peace process was now "clinically dead."
Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak and Syrian President Hafez al-Assad, speaking before the U.S. announcement, said they were not optimistic about a resumption soon of the peace process.
Mubarak, after four hours of talks with Assad in the Red Sea resort Sharm el-Sheikh, said:

"We are all wondering how to move the peace process forward before it becomes buried...We can see that there are problems between the U.S. and Israel in this issue but we are giving it time in the hope that the U.S. can achieve something with Israel."
Assad, whose country has not held peace talks with Israel since Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu came to power in June, said "the doors of peace are closed."
Kanafani told a news conference: "Bascially the peace process now is clinically dead and it is in the interests of Israel and the Palestinians to return to the negotiating table."
He welcomed the return of Ross, saying: "We hope he will come back with tangible ideas that will help President Arafat and Prime Minister Netanyahu return to the negotiating table."

The trip will be Ross's second to the Middle East in two months. After he returns to Washington, President Bill Clinton will make "some judgements about how the United States can best help the parties make progress," State Department spokesman John Dinger said.

Netanyahu's green light on groundbreaking for a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem on March 18 and a bomb attack that killed a Palestinian militant and three Israeli women in a Tel Aviv cafe three days later halted Israel-PLO talks.

Kanafani said the Palestinians were prepared to restart peace talks as long as they first focused on settlement activities, which the PLO demands Netanyahu stop, and further Israeli withdrawals in the West Bank.
"After these issues are resolved, there will be a full resumption of the negotiations," Kanafani said.
Netanyahu has vowed to press ahead with the East Jerusalem project at Jabal Abu Ghneim, called Har Homa by Israel.

The Palestinian Authority views the plan to build 6,500 homes for Jews at the site as an Israeli attempt to prejudge the final status of Jerusalem before talks on a permanent peace agreement are held.

On Wednesday, Netanyahu renewed his proposal to enter immediately into so-called final-status negotiations with the Palestinians, who have rejected the offer as an attempt to avoid implementing West Bank pullbacks under interim peace deals.

The tough "final-settlement" issues include Palestinian refugees, Jewish settlers in occupied lands, borders and the future of East Jerusalem, captured by Israel in 1967 and annexed but claimed by both sides.
Netanyahu has also made a resumption of negotiations with the self-rule administration conditional on Arafat clamping down on Moslem militants and "terrorism".
Kanafani said the Palestininan Authority had resumed security cooperation with Israel, in meetings attended by U.S. officials.
"Now that the security coordination has been restored, it is up to Israel to resolve the crisis," he said.
But Kanafani said there would be no movement on the diplomatic front with Israel until Ross arrived.
